title: Exercise 4:  Estimate precision and uncertainty
text:
This series of exercises focuses on the precision of estimates calculated from Labour Force Survey data, in other words the degree to which we can trust them to reflect the likely values in the population. In order to do this, we will compute similar measures as before - means and proportions but this time we will be focusing on their confidence intervals.
Learning objectives:

To be able to compute and interpret confidence intervals of earnings in the LFS;
To be able to assess the impact of weighting on weighting ;
To be able to interpret CIs for regional differences;
To be able to use published LFS design effects and apply them to your own estimates;



In this exercise we will be using Quarterly LFS data for October-December 2024.
To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: Quarterly Labour Force Survey, October - December, 2024.



We will assume that the working directory for this exercise - where syntax files and other materials will be located - will be a folder named LFS_exercises. Once you have downloaded the data, save it somewhere accessible inside LFS_exercises for example in a folder called `Data.
We can now begin analysing the data using R. First let’s load the packages that we are going to need:
Let’s open the dataset.
```{ open, eval=c(-2,-5)} #| echo: -1 #| eval: -2 setwd (“~/”) # setwd (“~/Dropbox/tmps”) setwd (“~/LFS_exercises”)


lfs_od24 <- read_dta( “Data/lfs/UKDA-9349-stata/stata/stata13/lfsp_od24_eul_pwt24.dta” )

To make data manipulation easier, let's create a data frame with just the variables we need for the exercise. We can also use this opportunity to  convert categorical variables  into factors in order to make them easier to understand.

```{ mydata}
dataex4 <- lfs_od24 |>
  select(PERSNO, PIWT24, PWT24,GRSSWK, INECAC05, ILODEFR,
         FTPT, HOURPAY, SEX,INDE07M,GOVTOF2 ) |>
  mutate(
         across(
         c(INECAC05:GOVTOF2),\(x) as_factor(x, "both")
               )
         ) |>
  droplevels()




In this exercise, we will be comparing the mean gross weekly earnings (GRSSWK) and their confidence intervals using weighted and unweighted estimates. As previously, we will be using the weighting variable specifically designed for earnings: PIWT24.
First, let’s examine gross weekly earnings and compute its unweighted mean:
### Raw data
summary(lfs_od24$GRSSWK)

### Removing non-response
summary(lfs_od24$GRSSWK[lfs_od24$GRSSWK>=0])

hist(lfs_od24$GRSSWK[lfs_od24$GRSSWK>=0],
     main= "Distribution  of weekly earnings, October-December 2024",
     xlab = "Gross weekly earnings (GBP)")

### Computing the mean
mw<-mean(lfs_od24$GRSSWK[lfs_od24$GRSSWK>=0],na.rm=T)

mw

Let’s now compute the confidence interval. We need to do it by hand, using the standard deviation sd() function.
s.mw<-sd(lfs_od24$GRSSWK[lfs_od24$GRSSWK>=0],na.rm=T)

s.mw
As a reminder, the 95% confidence interval of a mean is the value of the mean plus or minus 1.96 times its standard error. The standard error itself is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size:
```{ ci.u} lb<-mw-1.96(s.mw/sqrt(nrow(lfs_od24))) ub<-mw+1.96(s.mw/sqrt(nrow(lfs_od24)))
round(c(mw,lb,ub))
We can now say that on the basis of unweighted sample values, we could be 95% confident that the mean Gross Weekly earnings of the UK population overall range between £`{}  round(lb)` and £`{}  round(ub)` per week, that is an interval of  £`{}  round(ub)-round(lb)`.

Let's now look at the weighted estimates. We will be using the same survey data specific functions as in previous exercises.



```{ ci.w}
### Let's declare our data to be survey data with PIWT as weight. 
dataex4.s<-as_survey_design(weights=PIWT24,dataex4)
 
### ... Then get the weights 
mw.s<-dataex4.s|>
      summarise(survey_mean(GRSSWK,vartype = "ci"))

mw.s


QuestionsAnswers



What are the bounds between which we can be sure 95% of the values can be found, once we weight the data?
How wide is the weighted confidence interval?
What is the effect of weighting the data on the precision of estimates




It is between £{}  round(mw.s[2]) and £{}  round(mw.s[3]) per week
£{}  round(mw.s[3] - mw.s[2])
The confidence intervals of weighted value tends to be wider than that of unweighted estimates, which makes them at the same time more representative but less precise than unweighted ones.







In this second exercise, we will be looking at how to obtain and interpret confidence intervals of proportions by comparing the percentages of female employees in London and the North West of England. First, let’s examine the variable for regions:
table(dataex4$GOVTOF2)
Let’s recode the missing values in FTPT into system missing.
dataex4$FTPT2<-ifelse(dataex4$FTPT=="[1] Full time" | dataex4$FTPT=="[2] Part time",as.character(dataex4$FTPT),NA)
dataex4$FTPT2<-as.factor(dataex4$FTPT2)

### We recreate a weights informed survey design object
dataex4.s<-as_survey_design(weights=PWT24,dataex4)

ldn<-dataex4.s |>  
   filter(SEX=="[2] Female" & ILODEFR=="[1] In employment" & GOVTOF2=="[8] London") |> 
   group_by(FTPT2) |> 
   cascade(prop=survey_mean(vartype = "ci"))

nw<-dataex4.s |>  
   filter(SEX=="[2] Female" & 
          ILODEFR=="[1] In employment" & 
          GOVTOF2=="[2] North West") |> 
   group_by(FTPT2) |> 
   cascade(prop=survey_mean(vartype = "ci"))

### Raw results for London 
ldn


### Formatted results for the North West
round(100*
        nw |> 
        filter(FTPT2=="[2] Part time") |> 
        select(prop,prop_low,prop_upp),
      2) 


### Alternative method
100*svyby(
  ~I(FTPT2=="[2] Part time"),~(SEX=="[2] Female" &
                               ILODEFR=="[1] In employment" &
                               GOVTOF2=="[2] North West" ),
                              dataex4.s,
                              svyciprop,
                              vartype = "ci"
              )

QuestionsAnswers



Are the width of the confidence intervals for London and The North West comparable?
Do the CI overlap? How do you interpret this?
Is it the same with the differences between the North East and the North West of England?




Yes, they are very close at about 5 percentage points.
They don’t overlap, meaning that the difference are likely to be significant (at the 95% threshold) in the population
The confidence intervals clearly overlap. It is unlikely that significant difference in the proportion of female part-timers significantly differ between the two regions.

ne<-dataex4.s |>  
   filter(SEX=="[2] Female" & 
          ILODEFR=="[1] In employment" & 
          GOVTOF2=="[1] North East") |> 
   group_by(FTPT2) |> 
   cascade(prop=survey_mean(vartype = "ci"))

round(100*
        ne |> 
        filter(FTPT2=="[2] Part time") |> 
        select(prop,prop_low,prop_upp),
      2) 






Design effects account for the impact of survey design (e.g., clustering and stratification) on the precision of estimates. Here, we will be adjusting the CI of the proportion of women and men employed (ILODEFR) in manufacturing (INDE07M) in their main job using design effects published in Volume 1 of the LFS documentation.
Let’s begin by examining the sector variable:

cbind(Freq.=table(dataex4$INDE07M[dataex4$ILODEFR=="[1] In employment"]),
      Pct.=round(100*
            prop.table(
            table(dataex4$INDE07M[dataex4$ILODEFR=="[1] In employment"])),
            1)
      )
Let’s then compute the proportion of people employed in manufacturing:
fem<-dataex4.s |>  
   filter(SEX=="[2] Female" & 
          ILODEFR=="[1] In employment") |> 
   group_by(INDE07M=="[3] C -Manufacturing") |> 
   cascade(prop=survey_mean(vartype = "ci"))

mam<-dataex4.s |>  
   filter(SEX=="[1] Male" & 
          ILODEFR=="[1] In employment") |> 
   group_by(INDE07M=="[3] C -Manufacturing") |> 
   cascade(prop=survey_mean(vartype = "ci"))
… and examine the results for females:
round(100*fem,2)
… And males:
round(100*mam,2)
The above results are ‘naive’ confidence intervals ie confidence intervals that do not take into account survey design and depending on the case, maybe too narrow ie overstate the precision of the estimates - or too wide.
In order to compute more robust standard errors, we need to have access to survey design variables such as strata and primary sampling units identifiers, These are unfortunately withheld by the producers of the LFS< due to concerns about potential disclosure of personal information.
Another approach that can be implemented for some headline estimates consists in adapting confidence intervals based on the design factors (DEFF) published by the ONS. These can be in the the Volume 1 of the documentation. For the October-December edition of the LFS, this file is called: lfs_user_guide_vol1_background_2024.pdf.















The design effects for the proportion of female and males employed in manufacturing are respectively 1.2216 and 1.3048:















We now need to adapt these to the confidence intervals we computed earlier. In order to do this, we need our original standard errors - as the DEFF are meant to adjust these. We can then obtain the adjusted CIs for females:
sef<-dataex4.s |>  
   filter(SEX=="[2] Female" & 
          ILODEFR=="[1] In employment") |> 
   group_by(INDE07M=="[3] C -Manufacturing") |> 
   cascade(prop=survey_mean(vartype = "se"))

round(
c(100*sef$prop[2],
100*sef$prop[2]-1.96*sqrt(sef$prop_se[2]*1.2216),
100*sef$prop[2]+1.96*sqrt(sef$prop_se[2]*1.2216)
),2
)
… Then for males:
sem<-dataex4.s |>  
   filter(SEX=="[1] Male" & 
          ILODEFR=="[1] In employment") |> 
   group_by(INDE07M=="[3] C -Manufacturing") |> 
   cascade(prop=survey_mean(vartype = "se"))

round(
c(100*sem$prop[2],
100*sem$prop[2]-1.96*sqrt(sem$prop_se[2]*1.3048),
100*sem$prop[2]+1.96*sqrt(sem$prop_se[2]*1.3048)
),2
)

QuestionsAnswers



What has happened to the confidence intervals after we adjusted them?
What if we wanted to adjust our earlier estimates of gross weekly earnings for the design effects?



1.They have narrowed, which means that in this case, taking the survey design into account improves the precision of estimates.
2. We would not be able to do this with the safeguarded version of the data. We would need to use the secured version, and compute the adjusted estimates ourselves.

title: Estimates of temporary employment
text:
Weighted and unweighted frequencies
In order to provide reliable estimates of population values, survey data needs to be weighted when analysed. Weights are variables whose values increase or decrease the relative importance of observations, depending on how likely respondents were to take part to the survey. Some weights are only designed to correct the relative importance of observations, whereas others in addition also enable calculating population totals - the latter are called grossing weights.
Below, we compare weighted and unweighted frequencies and percentages.
We will be using Stata’s specially designed survey commands.

title: Confidence Intervals with UK LFS (Oct-Dec 2023)
text:
This worksheet will guide you through working with confidence intervals (CIs) using the UK Quarterly Labour Force Survey (LFS) October-December 2023 data (od24). You will learn how to compare weighted and unweighted estimates, compare weighted CIs across regions, and adjust CIs using design effects.




In survey data, weighting is often used to ensure that estimates are representative of the population. Here, we compare the weighted and unweighted estimates of mean gross weekly earnings (GRSSWK) and their confidence intervals. The weighting variable is PIWT24.




# Load necessary libraries
library(survey)
library(dplyr)
library(haven)

od24 <- read_dta(
        "~/Data/lfs/UKDA-9349-stata/stata/stata13/lfsp_od24_eul_pwt24.dta"
                    )

# Calculate unweighted mean and CI
unweighted_mean <- mean(od24$GRSSWK, na.rm = TRUE)
unweighted_ci <- t.test(od24$GRSSWK)$conf.int

# Create survey design object
lfs_design <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~PIWT24, data = od24)

# Calculate weighted mean and CI
weighted_mean <- svymean(~GRSSWK, design = lfs_design, na.rm = TRUE)
weighted_ci <- confint(weighted_mean)





# Print results
cat("Unweighted Mean:", unweighted_mean, "\n")

Unweighted Mean: 75.80171 

cat("Unweighted CI:", unweighted_ci, "\n")

Unweighted CI: 73.33218 78.27124 

cat("Weighted Mean:", weighted_mean, "\n")

Weighted Mean: 693.7501 

cat("Weighted CI:", weighted_ci, "\n")

Weighted CI: 681.8465 705.6538 





The unweighted mean and CI do not account for the survey design, while the weighted mean and CI use the weighting variable PIWT24 to produce representative estimates. The weighted CI is typically wider due to the incorporation of design effects.




Why is the weighted CI wider than the unweighted CI?
What does the weighting variable PIWT24 represent?
How might ignoring weights affect the interpretation of the results?





The weighted CI is wider because it accounts for the survey design, including stratification and clustering, which increases the variability of the estimate.
PIWT24 is the person-level weight for the survey, ensuring the sample represents the population.
Ignoring weights can lead to biased estimates that do not reflect the true population parameters.








In this exercise, we compare the weighted confidence intervals of the proportion of female employees who self-reported working part-time (FTPT) in London and the North West. The regional variable is GOVTOF2.




# Filter data for females and part-time workers
female_parttime <- od24 %>% filter(SEX == 2 & FTPT == 2)

# Create survey design object
lfs_design <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~PIWT24, data = female_parttime)

# Calculate weighted proportions and CIs for London and North West
london_prop <- svymean(~GOVTOF2 == 7, design = lfs_design)
northwest_prop <- svymean(~GOVTOF2 == 2, design = lfs_design)

london_ci <- confint(london_prop)
northwest_ci <- confint(northwest_prop)





# Print results
cat("London Proportion:", london_prop, "\n")

London Proportion: 0.9089568 0.09104316 

cat("London CI:", london_ci, "\n")

London CI: 0.8916423 0.07372865 0.9262713 0.1083577 

cat("North West Proportion:", northwest_prop, "\n")

North West Proportion: 0.8962006 0.1037994 

cat("North West CI:", northwest_ci, "\n")

North West CI: 0.8774707 0.08506962 0.9149304 0.1225293 





The weighted proportions and CIs show the estimated proportion of female part-time workers in London and the North West. The CIs provide a range within which the true proportion is likely to lie.




What does the overlap (or lack thereof) between the CIs for London and the North West indicate?
How does the sample size in each region affect the width of the CI?
Why is it important to use weights when comparing regions?





Overlapping CIs suggest no statistically significant difference between the proportions, while non-overlapping CIs indicate a significant difference.
Larger sample sizes result in narrower CIs, as they provide more precise estimates.
Weights ensure that the estimates are representative of the population in each region, accounting for differences in sampling probabilities.








Design effects account for the impact of survey design (e.g., clustering and stratification) on the precision of estimates. Here, we adjust the CI of the proportion of people in employment (ILODEFR) by age bands (AGE) using design effects published in Volume 1 of the LFS documentation.




# Load design effects for age bands
design_effects <- c(1.2, 1.5, 1.8) # Example values for age bands 16-24, 25-34, 35+

# Create survey design object
lfs_design <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~PIWT24, data = od24)

# Calculate weighted proportions and CIs by age band
age_props <- svyby(~ILODEFR == 1, ~AGE, design = lfs_design, svymean)

# Adjust CIs using design effects
adjusted_cis <- confint(age_props) * sqrt(design_effects)












The adjusted CIs account for the design effects, which increase the width of the CIs to reflect the reduced precision due to the survey design. This provides a more accurate measure of uncertainty.




What is a design effect, and why is it important?
How do design effects impact the width of the CI?
Why might design effects vary across age bands?





A design effect measures how much the survey design increases the variance of an estimate compared to a simple random sample. It is important because it ensures accurate uncertainty estimates.
Design effects increase the width of the CI, reflecting the reduced precision due to clustering and stratification.
Design effects vary across age bands due to differences in sample sizes, clustering, and stratification within each age group.






This worksheet has introduced you to working with confidence intervals in survey data, including weighting, regional comparisons, and design effects. Apply these techniques to your own analyses to ensure accurate and representative results. ```

title: Exercise 4:  Estimate precision and uncertainty
text:
This series of exercises focuses on the precision of estimates calculated from Labour Force Survey data, in other words the degree to which we can trust them to reflect the likely values in the population. In order to do this, we will compute similar measures as before - means and proportions but this time we will be focusing on their confidence intervals.
Learning objectives:

To be able to compute and interpret confidence intervals of earnings in the LFS;
To be able to assess the impact of weighting on weighting ;
To be able to interpret CIs for regional differences;
To be able to use published LFS design effects and apply them to your own estimates;



In this exercise we will be using Quarterly LFS data for October-December 2024.
To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: Quarterly Labour Force Survey, October - December, 2024.



We will assume that the working directory for this exercise - where syntax files and other materials will be located - will be a folder named LFS_exercises. Once you have downloaded the data, save it somewhere accessible inside LFS_exercises for example in a folder called `Data.
We can now begin analysing the data using R. First let’s load the packages that we are going to need:

library(haven)  ### Functions to open Stata or SPSS datasets
library(dplyr)  ### Easier data manipulation
library(survey) ### Survey data analysis functions
library(srvyr)  ### Easier  manipulation of survey data

Let’s open the dataset.

## setwd ("~/LFS_exercises")

### Importing a Stata format dataset
lfs_od24 <- read_dta(
        "Data/lfs/UKDA-9349-stata/stata/stata13/lfsp_od24_eul_pwt24.dta"
                    )

To make data manipulation easier, let’s create a data frame with just the variables we need for the exercise. We can also use this opportunity to convert categorical variables into factors in order to make them easier to understand.

dataex4 <- lfs_od24 |>
  select(PERSNO, PIWT24, PWT24,GRSSWK, INECAC05, ILODEFR,
         FTPT, HOURPAY, SEX,INDE07M,GOVTOF2 ) |>
  mutate(
         across(
         c(INECAC05:GOVTOF2),\(x) as_factor(x, "both")
               )
         ) |>
  droplevels()




In this exercise, we will be comparing the mean gross weekly earnings (GRSSWK) and their confidence intervals using weighted and unweighted estimates. As previously, we will be using the weighting variable specifically designed for earnings: PIWT24.
First, let’s examine gross weekly earnings and compute its unweighted mean:

### Raw data
summary(lfs_od24$GRSSWK)

   -9.0    -9.0    -9.0    75.8    -9.0 23076.0 

### Removing non-response

### Computing the mean
mw<-mean(lfs_od24$GRSSWK[lfs_od24$GRSSWK>=0],na.rm=T)

mw

[1] 732.4975


Let’s now compute the confidence interval. We need to do it by hand, using the standard deviation sd() function.

s.mw<-sd(lfs_od24$GRSSWK[lfs_od24$GRSSWK>=0],na.rm=T)

s.mw

[1] 623.6522


As a reminder, the 95% confidence interval of a mean is the value of the mean plus or minus 1.96 times its standard error. The standard error itself is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size:

lb<-mw-1.96*(s.mw/sqrt(nrow(lfs_od24)))
ub<-mw+1.96*(s.mw/sqrt(nrow(lfs_od24)))

round(c(mw,lb,ub))

[1] 732 728 737


We can now say that on the basis of unweighted sample values, we could be 95% confident that the mean Gross Weekly earnings of the UK population overall range between £728 and £737 per week, that is an interval of £9.

In this exercise, we will be comparing the mean gross weekly earnings (GRSSWK) and their confidence intervals using weighted and unweighted estimates. As previously, we will be using the weighting variable specifically designed for earnings: PIWT24.
First, let’s examine gross weekly earnings and compute its unweighted mean:

   -9.0    -9.0    -9.0    75.8    -9.0 23076.0 

### Removing non-response

    5.0   413.2   615.0   732.5   923.0 23076.0

     main= "Distribution  of weekly earnings, October-December 2024",
     xlab = "Gross weekly earnings (GBP)")







### Computing the mean
mw<-mean(lfs_od24$GRSSWK[lfs_od24$GRSSWK>=0],na.rm=T)

mw

[1] 732.4975


Let’s now compute the confidence interval. We need to do it by hand, using the standard deviation sd() function.

s.mw<-sd(lfs_od24$GRSSWK[lfs_od24$GRSSWK>=0],na.rm=T)

s.mw

[1] 623.6522


As a reminder, the 95% confidence interval of a mean is the value of the mean plus or minus 1.96 times its standard error. The standard error itself is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size:

lb<-mw-1.96*(s.mw/sqrt(nrow(lfs_od24)))
ub<-mw+1.96*(s.mw/sqrt(nrow(lfs_od24)))

round(c(mw,lb,ub))

[1] 732 728 737


We can now say that on the basis of unweighted sample values, we could be 95% confident that the mean Gross Weekly earnings of the UK population overall range between £728 and £737 per week, that is an interval of £9.
Let’s now look at the weighted estimates. We will be using the same survey data specific functions as in previous exercises.

### Let's declare our data to be survey data with PIWT as weight. 
dataex4.s<-as_survey_design(weights=PIWT24,dataex4)
 
### ... Then get the weights

      summarise(survey_mean(GRSSWK,vartype = "ci"))

mw.s

  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1  694.   682.   706.

What are the bounds between which we can be sure 95% of the values can be found, once we weight the data?
How wide is the weighted confidence interval?
What is the effect of weighting the data on the precision of estimates




It is between £682 and £706 per week
£24
The confidence intervals of weighted value tends to be wider than that of unweighted estimates, which makes them at the same time more representative but less precise than unweighted ones.
